newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Baht bears awake as Thai finance minister quits.
newsitem.headline: Baht bears awake as Thai finance minister quits.

text.p: Bearish market operators awoke from an uneasy slumber on Thursday to take a fresh look at the baht following the resignation of Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan.
Currency hard-liner Amnuay was firmly in the no-devaluation camp and his departure put fresh downward pressure on the baht and gave Thai stocks another whack in the solar plexus.
But analysts in Singapore ruled out a baht devaluation, saying Amnuay leaves behind an equally hard-line central bank.
His departure followed conflict with political rivals in the ruling coalition over his handling of the ailing Thai economy, although he did have the confidence of financial markets.
"He was a person that was well respected by the markets and was a major driving force in trying to turn the economy around," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.
"This news is bad for the market all round ... people are again putting on new short positons against the baht."
Thai Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee, a member of Amnuay's economics team, said he would also resign.

The immediate knee-jerk reaction for the baht was down, with the offshore rate sinking to an early 25.0000/0300 against 23.5300/6300 late on Wednesday. Beleagured Thai stocks dropped more than three percent to their lowest level in over six years.
"There is no way to put this in a good light," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currencies research at BZW in Singapore.
"Amnuay prioritised macro-economic stability over maximising economic growth. There is no obvious candidate who has his credibility in the market."

In the run-up to Amnuay's resignation, the baht soared to a 16-year high against the dollar as speculators scrambled frantically to cover short postions taken out during an attack on the currency in mid-May.

Players dived for cover after a savaging by the Bank of Thailand which, in answer to the speculative attack, slapped on currency controls and cut off local sources of baht supply to foreigners. Liquidity dried up and the baht rocketed.
"The Bank of Thailand certainly won the battle for the baht and it remains to be seen whether they can win the war," said one trader at a European bank here. "And now they have lost a valuable ally."
"But a lot of people lost a lot of money and they will be wary of shorting it agressively again. We've already seen the forwards come right back from today's initial levels," he added.
Analysts doubt very much the Thai authorities will sanction a drop in the value of the baht. With the economy growing around six percent, a devaluation would fuel import inflation.
But more important is the high level of offshore debt and a devaluation would probably send a large number of unhedged, U.S. dollar indebted Thai firms and finance houses out of business.
So analysts said they expected the status quo to be maintained in the coming months and the Bank of Thailand to fight tooth and nail to protect the value of the baht.

While further short-term measures would undoubtedly burn speculators, analysts said it was vitally important for the Thai authorities to concentrate on winning back the confidence of financial markets.

"They have to look like they are managing the business cycle and managing the structural problems not just today's baht crisis," said Kobus Van Der Wath, regional head of treasury economics at Standard Chartered here.
"There is a baht crisis today because there are medium and longer term concerns. You have to look at the symptoms but you also need to look at the underlying cause of the disease."
